claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is governed by dislocation stability and mobility.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials is governed by dislocation stability and mobility.
Grain-boundary structure influences dislocation stability and mobility.
Solute distribution influences dislocation stability and mobility.
Controlled alloying and thermal processing can alter grain-boundary cohesion and solute segregation.
Grain-boundary cohesion affects the ability of dislocations to move and interact.
Solute segregation affects the ability of dislocations to move and interact.
Dislocation motion and interactions govern plastic strain and toughness.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion reduces dislocation pile-up.
An optimized solute distribution reduces dislocation pile-up.
Reduced dislocation pile-up promotes high-temperature ductility.
Materials with modified grain boundaries and solute distributions will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain than an unmodified baseline.
Materials with modified grain boundaries and solute distributions will exhibit greater high-temperature toughness than an unmodified baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to polycrystalline materials with grain sizes from 1 to 100 micrometers and solute concentrations below their high-temperature solubility limits.
Temperatures above 1000°C are representative of relevant fusion-reactor high-temperature conditions.
